report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true**. High-quality clinical evidence demonstrates that preoperative skin antisepsis with **chlorhexidine-alcohol** significantly reduces the risk of surgical-site infection (SSI) after cesarean delivery compared with **iodine-alcohol** (and aqueous povidone-iodine).

### Summary of Evidence
* **Landmark Randomized Controlled Trial:** A major pragmatic randomized trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Tuuli et al.) evaluated 1,147 women undergoing elective or non-elective cesarean delivery. Skin preparation with chlorhexidine-alcohol led to a significantly lower rate of SSI compared with iodine-alcohol (4.0% vs. 7.3%; relative risk 0.55), substantially reducing both superficial and deep incisional infections.
* **Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses:** Subsequent meta-analyses comparing preoperative skin antiseptics for cesarean section confirm that chlorhexidine-alcohol consistently outperforms povidone-iodine formulations in preventing SSIs and suppressing skin bacterial colonization.
* **Clinical Guidelines:** Major professional bodies, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), recommend alcohol-based skin preparations prior to cesarean delivery and favor chlorhexidine-alcohol due to its rapid bactericidal onset and persistent antimicrobial activity on skin.

### Sources
* *New England Journal of Medicine* Trial: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048
* Meta-Analysis in PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/
* Systematic Review in ScienceDirect: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282
* Clinical Practice Guidance Summary: https://www.obgproject.com/2018/09/30/chlorhexidine-or-iodine-based-skin-prep-for-cesarean-sections/
